newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-OLD FOES MEET AGAIN IN WORLD CUP QUALIFIERS. [corrected 11:37 gmt 14/12]
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-OLD FOES MEET AGAIN IN WORLD CUP QUALIFIERS. [corrected 11:37 gmt 14/12]

text.p: Neighbours square up to one another and club team mates become international rivals on Saturday as six of Europe's leading soccer nations face their toughest match yet on the road to the 1998 World Cup finals.

The Netherlands face neighbours Belgium in what has become an almost permanent fixture on the World Cup calendar while Spain meet a Yugoslav squad boasting eight players who earn their keep in the Spanish league.
In the other big tie of the weekend Germany travel to Portugal seeking revenge against the only side to have beaten them in a World Cup qualifier.
The Dutch and the Belgians must be sick of the sight of each other.

This will be the eighth World Cup in which the Benelux neighbours have crossed swords since their first encounter in the tournament in 1934 when the Netherlands won 4-2. Their last World Cup clash was in the United States in 1994, the Belgians winning 1-0 (corrects from "The Dutch winning 1-0").
Saturday's group seven clash will be the 118th meeting between the two sides and the Dutch, who have won 53 times to Belgium's 39, sense victory again.
"There's absolutely no reason to be afraid," said Netherlands defender Frank de Boer. "We should be able to beat Belgium."
"The Netherlands are better," team mate Jaap Stam added confidently.
Spain and Yugoslavia know each other better than most, too. This is the sixth World Cup in which they have been matched, all of them since 1970.
Added to that, eight of the Yugoslav squad play against Spaniards week in week out for their club sides.

Striker Pedrag Mijatovic could find himself face to face with Real Madrid team mate Rafael Alkorta, Atletico Madrid's Kiko Narvaez and Milinko Pantic will be on opposite sides, and Deportivo Coruna's Miroslav Djukic may be up against club team mate Javier Manjarin.
Even the president of the Yugoslav Football Federation, Miljan Miljanic, used to be at Real Madrid and still speaks good Spanish.
If history is anything to go by Yugoslavia have the most to fear from Saturday's group six clash in Valencia.
Their 2-1 win over Spain in the 1990 finals in Italy -- the last time the two sides met in the competition -- was their first World Cup triumph over the Spanish in nine matches.
The game will be especially poignant for former Valencia player Mijatovic who has had a tumultuous December.

Ten days ago he saw his young son rushed to hospital for an emergency operation. Three days later he led Real to victory over arch-rivals Barcelona and now the striker will encounter not only some of his team mates but also his former fans in the Mediterranean city.
Germany's memories of Portugal are less extensive but no less intense.
Portugal's 1-0 win in Stuttgart in 1985 remains the only World Cup qualifying match the Germans have lost and Berti Vogts' side travel to Lisbon with revenge high on the agenda.

But the Germans, held 1-1 by unfancied Northern Ireland in their last group nine match, have three doubtful Thomases -- midfielder Thomas Haessler and defenders Thomas Helmer and Thomas Strunz, who are all injured.
"The fact that players are missing is no excuse if we don't put on a decent show on Saturday. We don't have 'reserve' players," Vogts said.
German confidence will be boosted by the return of libero Matthias Sammer, making his first appearance for the national side since his brilliant performances in the European championship in June.
